listenings.text: Just after midnight, the screen in front of him reported a launch. Then a second. In the end, five. Now, the system was new, it had cost an enormous amount of money, and it was saying, in effect, that a war had started. His instructions were not ambiguous. Report it upwards, immediately. And he had, at the outside, four minutes. What he did instead was think about the number. Five missiles. If you were opening a war of that kind, you would not send five. You would send hundreds. And so he decided, on that reasoning alone, that the system was wrong, and he waited. It was wrong. The satellite had misread sunlight on high cloud. The world found out about all of this ten years later, by accident, from a memoir.

I am going to argue against my own colleagues for a moment. The trouble with counterfactual history is not that it is frivolous. It is that it cannot be tested. Whatever you propose, I can propose the opposite with exactly the same confidence, and the argument is then decided by whoever tells the better story, which is not a standard of evidence. That said, I do not think it is worthless. Done carefully, it does one thing extremely well: it reminds you that the outcome you are studying was contingent, and that the people living through it did not know how it ended. So here is my rule, and I offer it seriously. Change one thing. Only one. And change it as late as possible, because the further back you go, the more you are simply writing fiction.

extra_audio.text: Vera says her students want a hero and dislike the broken satellite in the story. He points out that with the other officer on duty the conversation might be very different now. She explains that procedure required a report and that he waited instead. He asks whether it was judgement or a fluke, since the lessons differ. She answers that it was both, and that the word probably is doing an enormous amount of work.
